content:
ASHE COUNTY — The mountains of northwest North Carolina conjure lore steeped in tradition while casting a wary eye on superstition, an ingrained, foreboding testament to a reckoning with the supernatural.

Relatives and neighbors pass down ghost stories like heirloom quilts. The origin and authenticity of ghoulish accounts matter less than the lasting impression and posterity. Haints in the holler, roadside devils, or the apocryphal lady in white, drifting over sullen mountain cemeteries, are Ashe County’s haunted houses. Appalachia offers no admission or gatekeeping for the unknown; only trepidation or outright dismissal of the unexplained dispels the County’s lore, at the risk of losing out on local mystique.

Where logic fails, the macabre and metaphysical transcend an inherent repulsion of the vile and wicked - nothing gets in the way of a good story or dare on a cool autumn night. Sleuthing the spiritual and forbidden domains always comes with a safety net. Belief lends credence to Appalachia’s cryptids and haunted past. Alas, the motif of memory keepers - preserving another mountain tradition like canned beans and old wives’ tales.

Spooky season doesn’t go out of style in ancient Appalachia. Darkened valleys, dense forests, and eerily quiet ridgelines are as eternal as they are ephemeral; only daybreak offers reprieve from the night's mysteries.

Ashe County’s ghost stories are well documented and preserved, with only anecdotal interpretation hijacking the narrative. While subjectivity derides and misconstrues the haunted hills, enduring legends ignite the imagination. Naysayers are poor storytellers. Diving into Ashe County’s haunted past is a living history of the undead who can’t move past the unknown or leave their mountain homes, kept alive by vivid accounts like a bad dream unspoiled by objectivity.

Ashe County’s haunted history isn’t urban legend. It’s a rural reckoning and an Appalachian appreciation for a complicated past.

The Devil’s Stairs

Perhaps Ashe County’s most enduring paranormal story is the legend of the Devil’s Stairs in Warrensville on N.C. 88.

The legend began with a blast, the spark that keeps the story alive and piques the malleable minds of lovers of the unknown.

The jagged rock protrusion, supposedly rising from the depths of Hell, is connected to the Norfolk & Western Railway track extension from Abingdon, Va., into Ashe County in 1914. Dynamiters blasted a section of rock at the river bend, leveling a formation that resembled large steps leading up the side of the mountain. Incipient legend dubiously links the blast shaping the stairs to the death of a construction worker killed in the dynamite blast, according to newrivernotes.com.

Versions of the forthcoming folklore or mountain ghost story vary as much as the road’s twists and turns as it meanders into Creston. One version centers on a stalled car at the stairs: a back door opens, the devil enters the vehicle, and quickly exits—a demonic spark that finally turns the engine over.

Another account, which ran in the Jefferson Post’s bicentennial edition, more succinctly retells a blood-curdling run-in with forces darker than any mountain holler.

“As the car neared the Devil’s Stairs, the minister saw a hitchhiker in a dark black raincoat that covered his head and face,” the story later reshared in local online forums says. “The preacher stopped to offer the stranger a lift, primarily out of compassion due to the raw weather that evening. ‘The hitchhiker did not say a word as he sat in the back seat,’ the account says. The reverend checked the rear-view mirror several times but never saw the hitchhiker’s face. So he turned around and looked into the man’s eyes, which were as red as fire and as big as a fist.’ The startled minister pulled over to the side of the road to let the rider out, but when he got out and opened the back door, he found no one inside the car.”

The Lady in White

The ‘Lady in the White Dress’ ghost story isn’t unique to Ashe County, as timeless variations find a malleable audience worldwide.

Ashe County’s version centers on a Lady in White at the Howell Hill Cemetery in Lansing, a popular “parking spot” for teenagers, according to a previous Jefferson Post special section.

Graveside smoochers often reported seeing a lady in a white or translucent dress rise from the ground, appearing to float among the gravestones with a flowing accent despite the lack of wind. Startled parkers, fumbling with their keys and hijacked by adrenaline after a failed conquest, started their cars to leave when they felt a cold draft enter the car. The horror-stricken teenagers, who experienced a full spectrum of emotions from adulating trysts to conjuring love’s diametric foe, then saw the white-clad lady sitting in the backseat, only to disappear when the car stopped, according to the paper’s retelling.

Museum of ghostly mayhem

Before the Museum of Ashe County History encapsulated the county’s illustrious past with erudite rotating exhibits, the 1904 building was the county’s courthouse, the prime venue for gavel-swinging gossip and hearsay.

While jurisprudence was the objective, the tainted energy of injustice and altered lives, unceremoniously adjudicated as abject humiliation in front of neighbors and friends, left an indelible, haunted legacy.

Corroborating the legend with modern advances, a paranormal investigation team entered the old courthouse in 2011 to investigate the claims. The group recorded audio evidence, including a voice saying "Order!", the sound of a gavel banging, heavy footsteps, and breathing in the main upstairs courtroom.

Haunted afterthoughts

Ashe County’s best haunted rest beguiles with blood-curdling undertones.

The old county hospital is a likely setting for paranormal activity, as the countless patients hanging on the eternal precipice of death and convalescence undoubtedly imbued the building with residual spiritual fetters.

Constructed in 1939, the building served as Ashe County’s hospital, meaning that a great number of people would have died inside the building while it was in operation. The building was later converted into a county office in 1969 and eventually shut down.

The dark rooms and macabre atmosphere made the old hospital an ideal haunted-house setting. Dr. Leigh Bradley of High Country Family Medicine was one of the volunteers who set up the first haunted house in 2010.

“That was a freaky place to be in,” Bradley said in a previous interview. “I didn’t like being alone in there during broad daylight; forget about being alone in there after dark, and I’m pretty brave.”

They had to add artificial power and lighting inside the old hospital while setting up the haunted house.

According to Bradley, the lights went out every night at about 10 p.m.

Due to how spooky this was, Bradley decided to stop setting up her room after dark, and her experiences were fewer than her fellow volunteers’.

According to Bradley, several of her peers saw orbs of light briefly floating through the dark halls.

Others reported hearing an elevator and a bell, even though the building's power had long been shut down.

Bradley said the volunteers even played a game, challenging each other to see how far they would walk into the uncharted parts of the old hospital before turning back. Even with a flashlight in hand, no one went more than 20 feet into the hospital alone.

“The main thing is there is just a really spooky feeling you get in the hospital ... there are rooms where you would go into them and get the most amazing chill,” Bradley said. “The paranormal investigators (3P Paranormal) actually spent the night in there, which is more than I would have done.”

“If there really is such a thing as a haunted building in the whole world, it’s that hospital,” Bradley said.
